CausalChain: Chronic liver injury/inflammation -> Activation of hepatic stellate cells -> Increased secretion of HGF -> Activation of MET signaling in hepatocytes -> Oncogenic transformation and increased AFP-L3 production -> Enhanced tumor aggressiveness and vascular invasion
Hypothesis: In HCC, inhibiting hepatic stellate cell-derived HGF will reduce MET pathway activation, leading to decreased AFP-L3 production and tumor aggressiveness, thereby offering a novel therapeutic strategy to improve patient outcomes.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by a complex interplay between chronic liver injury, stromal activation, and tumor cell evolution, leading to aggressive disease phenotypes. In this context, hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) activated by chronic inflammation secrete hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), which in turn stimulates the MET signaling pathway in hepatocytes. This study hypothesizes that HGF-mediated MET activation promotes not only tumor proliferation but also the preferential production of the AFP-L3 isoform – a biomarker associated with aggressive tumor behavior. Therefore, targeting HGF secretion from activated HSCs may attenuate MET-driven oncogenic signaling and diminish AFP-L3 expression, offering a novel therapeutic angle to curb tumor aggressiveness and improve HCC outcomes. This hypothesis advocates for a dual biomarker and therapeutic approach where modulation of the tumor microenvironment alters circulating biomarker profiles and, concomitantly, clinical prognoses.
